narrative:
The model predicted an 84% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a high bar for admission, this probability led to your application being rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your class rank at the end of your third year was the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) while students who were accepted averaged around the middle of their class (5.8). Your first-year class rank was the second most important factor and also pulled the prediction toward failure; you ranked in the second decile compared to an average of sixth decile among accepted students. Your LSAT score was the third most important factor and likewise increased the chance of failure. A score of 30 sits noticeably below the 37-point average of admitted students.

Taken together, these academic performance signals outweighed other details such as your undergraduate GPA of 3.2 (nearly identical to the accepted average), your lower-middle family income, and your plan to attend full-time.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic record and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score. Many students successfully reapply after targeted improvement in these areas.
